title: Liberalism

cards.h: The ideology that built the modern world
cards.b:
Liberalism is the dominant ideology of the modern West and the base of most written constitutions, including India's. It puts the individual first and asks what limits should bind the state.

It is also the ideology that the others argue with. Marxists attack its idea of the market. Conservatives attack its optimism about reason. Feminists attack its public-private split. Communitarians attack its view of the self.

In Paper I, expect questions on classical versus modern liberalism, the neoliberal turn, negative and positive liberty, and liberal critiques. Gauba, Heywood and Bhargava are the standard sources.

• Individualism: the individual is prior to society and has equal moral worth.
  • Liberty: freedom is the supreme political value. Interference needs justification.
  • Reason: people can improve their lives by using reason, so progress is possible.
  • Equality: formal equality before law and equal rights. Liberals disagree on how far to go beyond it.
  • Limited government and consent: power must rest on consent (social contract), be bound by law and be divided (rule of law, constitutionalism, separation of powers).

To these add toleration (rooted in the religious wars, Locke's Letter Concerning Toleration, 1689) and, in most forms, a market economy with private property.

cards.h: From classical to modern to neoliberal
cards.b:
Liberalism is not one doctrine but a family. It changed as industrial capitalism produced poverty and conflict.

  • Classical: free markets, minimal state, "negative" liberty.
  • Modern (also called social or welfare liberalism): the state should enable people to be free, with education, health and social security.
  • Neoliberal: a return to markets and a smaller state, from the 1970s.

cards.h: Classical liberals: Locke, Smith, Bentham, Mill
cards.b:
John Locke, Two Treatises of Government (1689)

Natural rights to life, liberty and property. Government exists by consent to protect them. If it betrays this trust, people may resist.

Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations (1776)

Market exchange, guided by the "invisible hand", can serve the public good. The state's tasks are defence, justice and certain public works.

J.S. Mill, On Liberty (1859)

The harm principle: the only reason to interfere with a person's liberty against their will is to prevent harm to others. Free speech matters even when the opinion is false, because it tests truth. Mill also showed how classical liberalism begins to turn social: he backed women's rights and worker cooperatives.

Bentham's utilitarianism served as another base for reform and for the rule of law.

By the late 19th century, industrial poverty made "freedom of contract" look hollow to many. Modern liberals redefined liberty.

  • T.H. Green (1836-82), the British idealist, argued that real freedom is the power to do something worthwhile. The state should remove obstacles such as ignorance and squalor. This is the root of positive liberty in liberal thought.
  • L.T. Hobhouse, Liberalism (1911), defended social reform.
  • J.M. Keynes, The General Theory (1936), said governments should manage demand to prevent mass unemployment.
  • William Beveridge's 1942 report planned the British welfare state.

The American New Deal (1930s) and the post-war welfare state were the practical results. Rawls and Dworkin are the best-known modern liberal philosophers.

Isaiah Berlin, "Two Concepts of Liberty" (1958), gave the standard terms.

Negative liberty

Freedom from interference. How much area is left free? Classical liberals and libertarians prefer it.

Positive liberty

Freedom to be self-directed and fulfil one's potential. It asks about the conditions of choice, like education and income.

Berlin feared the positive view could be abused. A ruler might claim to know people's "true self" and force them to be free. Soviet and fascist states did just that, he thought. He defended negative liberty as safer and admitted that values like liberty and equality can conflict (value pluralism).

The 1970s brought stagflation and doubts about Keynes. Thinkers revived market liberalism.

  • F.A. Hayek, The Road to Serfdom (1944) and The Constitution of Liberty (1960): central planning ends in tyranny. Prices carry knowledge no planner can have. "Social justice" is a mirage.
  • Milton Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom (1962): economic freedom is a condition of political freedom. He backed monetarism and school vouchers.
  • Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974): the minimal state only.

In politics, this became Thatcherism (UK, from 1979) and Reaganism (USA, from 1981), and later the "Washington Consensus": privatisation, deregulation, trade opening and fiscal discipline.

• Marxist: liberal rights, such as property and contract, hide class power. Formal equality sits on top of economic inequality (Marx, On the Jewish Question, 1844).
  • Conservative: abstract individualism ignores tradition and community (Burke, Oakeshott).
  • Communitarian: the liberal self is "unencumbered" (Sandel, MacIntyre).
  • Feminist: the public-private divide leaves the family outside justice (Okin; Pateman, The Sexual Contract, 1988).
  • Multicultural and postcolonial: liberalism claims universality but carried empire. Mill defended British rule in India for "backward" peoples.
  • Environmental: endless growth conflicts with ecological limits.

Defenders reply that liberalism can absorb these challenges, as modern liberalism did with welfare and rights.

• Early liberals: Raja Ram Mohan Roy, then the Moderates in Congress (Naoroji, Gokhale, Ranade), who sought constitutional reform. The National Liberal Federation was set up in 1919.
  • Constitution: Preamble (liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship), fundamental rights in Part III, judicial review and independent courts. Yet it mixes liberal rights with socialist directives in Part IV.
  • Economy: Nehru's mixed economy until 1991, when the July 1991 reforms (Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh) brought liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation.
  • Courts: Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down Section 66A of the IT Act on free speech. K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) made privacy a fundamental right. Navtej Singh Johar (2018) decriminalised consensual same-sex relations.

Since the 2008 financial crisis, liberalism has faced doubts. Populist movements have grown, inequality has risen in many states, and some leaders speak of "illiberal democracy" (a phrase popularised by Fareed Zakaria, 1997, and used by Viktor Orban in 2014).

Defenders, such as Fukuyama in Liberalism and Its Discontents (2022), argue that liberalism needs to be renewed, not abandoned. Critics like Patrick Deneen, Why Liberalism Failed (2018), say its individualism wore away community.

For the exam, a balanced answer notes that liberalism has changed repeatedly and that its core, the protection of individual rights under law, remains attractive and contested.

"Liberalism is a political ideology in transition." Discuss.
Distinguish between classical and modern liberalism.
Examine the neoliberal critique of the welfare state.
Explain the concepts of negative and positive liberty. Which is more important?

Structure: define liberalism by its core ideas. Trace the three phases with thinkers and books. Use Berlin to deal with liberty. Present the critiques from the left, the right, communitarians and feminists. Add India: the Preamble and Part III, 1991, and the privacy and speech cases. End with a verdict on whether liberalism is adaptable.

quiz.q: Who gave the terms negative and positive liberty their standard form?
The shift to modern liberalism is associated with…
quiz.w: Green argued the state should remove obstacles to real freedom.

quiz.q: The Road to Serfdom (1944) argues that…
Capitalism and Freedom (1962) was written by…
Which book is Keynes's key work?
quiz.w: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money, 1936.

quiz.q: The Sexual Contract (1988), a feminist critique of liberal contract theory, is by…
quiz.w: Pateman argued that the social contract rests on a hidden sexual contract.

quiz.q: Which ruling made privacy a fundamental right in India?
Section 66A of the IT Act was struck down in…
o: Shreya Singhal v Union of India
quiz.w: Shreya Singhal (2015) held it violated Article 19(1)(a).

quiz.q: India's major economic liberalisation began in…
quiz.w: July 1991 under P.V. Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh.
